chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter III
paragraphs: Princess Mary postponed her departure. Sonya and the count tried to take Natasha's place but couldn't. They saw that she alone was able to keep her mother from spiraling into unreasoning despair. For three weeks Natasha stayed constantly at her mother's side, sleeping on a lounge chair in her room, making her eat and drink, and talking to her endlessly, because the mere sound of her tender, soothing voice calmed the countess.

The mother's wounded spirit could not heal. Petya's death had torn half her life away. When the news of his death arrived, she had been a fresh and vigorous woman of fifty, but a month later she emerged from her room a listless old woman with no interest in life. But the same blow that nearly killed the countess—this second blow—restored Natasha to life.

A spiritual wound caused by the rending of the spiritual body is like a physical wound, and strange as it may seem, just as a deep wound may heal and its edges join, both physical and spiritual wounds can only truly heal from within, through the vital force of life itself.

Natasha's wound healed in that way. She had believed her life was over, but her love for her mother unexpectedly showed her that the essence of life—love—was still alive within her. Love awoke, and so did life.

Prince Andrew's last days had drawn Princess Mary and Natasha together; this new sorrow brought them closer still. Princess Mary postponed her departure and for three weeks looked after Natasha as though she were a sick child. The weeks spent in her mother's bedroom had drained Natasha's physical strength.

One afternoon, noticing Natasha shivering with fever, Princess Mary took her to her own room and made her lie down on the bed. Natasha lay down, but when Princess Mary drew the blinds and turned to leave, she called her back.
"I don't want to sleep, Mary. Sit with me a little."
"You're tired—try to sleep."
"No, no. Why did you bring me away? She'll be asking for me."
"She's much better. She spoke so well today," said Princess Mary.
Natasha lay on the bed and in the semidarkness studied Princess Mary's face.

"Is she like him?" thought Natasha. "Yes, like him and yet not like him. But she is entirely her own person—strange, new, and unknown. And she loves me. What is in her heart? Everything good. But how? What does she think about? What does she think about me? Yes, she is wonderful!"
"Mary," she said timidly, drawing Princess Mary's hand toward her, "Mary, you mustn't think I'm wicked. You don't, do you? Mary darling, how I love you! Let's be the very best of friends."
And Natasha, embracing her, began kissing her face and hands, making Princess Mary feel shy but happy at this outpouring of feeling.

From that day a tender and passionate friendship—the kind that exists only between women—was established between Princess Mary and Natasha. They were constantly kissing and saying tender things to each other and spent most of their time together. When one left the room, the other grew restless and hurried to rejoin her. Together they felt more in harmony with each other than either felt when alone. A feeling stronger than friendship arose between them—an intense sense that life was only possible in each other's presence.

Sometimes they were silent for hours; other times, after they were already in bed, they would begin talking and continue until morning. They spoke mostly of the distant past. Princess Mary told of her childhood, her mother, her father, and her dreams; and Natasha, who had previously turned away from that life of devotion, submission, and the poetry of Christian self-sacrifice with passive incomprehension, now—feeling bound to Princess Mary by love—learned to appreciate her past too and to understand a side of life that had been entirely foreign to her. She did not think of applying submission and self-denial to her own life, for she was used to seeking other kinds of joy; but she understood and loved those previously incomprehensible virtues in someone else. For Princess Mary, listening to Natasha's stories of childhood and youth, an equally new and previously unknown side of life opened up: a belief in life and its pleasures.

Just as before, they never spoke of him, so as not to lower (as they felt) their exalted feelings by putting them into words. But this silence gradually—without their realizing it—caused them to begin forgetting him.

Natasha had grown thin and pale and physically so weak that everyone discussed her health, which pleased her. But sometimes she was suddenly overcome by fear—not only of death, but of sickness, weakness, and the loss of her looks—and she would involuntarily examine her bare arm, surprised at its thinness, and in the morning notice her drawn and, as it seemed to her, pitiful face in the mirror. It seemed to her that this was how things had to be, and yet it was terribly sad.

One day she ran quickly upstairs and found herself out of breath. Without thinking, she immediately invented a reason to go back down, and then, testing her strength, ran upstairs again, carefully noting the result.

Another time, when she called Dunyasha and her voice trembled, she called again—though she could hear Dunyasha coming—this time using the deep chest tones she used to sing with, and listened to herself attentively.

She did not know, and would not have believed, that beneath the layer of mud that seemed to her impenetrable, covering her soul, delicate young shoots of grass were already sprouting. They would take root and so cover with their living green the grief that weighed her down that it would soon no longer be seen or noticed. The wound had begun to heal from within.
At the end of January, Princess Mary left for Moscow, and the count insisted that Natasha go with her to see the doctors.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter IV
paragraphs: After the encounter at Vyazma, where Kutuzov had been unable to hold back his troops in their eagerness to overwhelm and cut off the enemy, the further movement of the fleeing French and the Russians who pursued them continued as far as Krasnoe without a battle. The flight was so rapid that the Russian army pursuing the French could not keep up; cavalry and artillery horses broke down, and the information about French movements was never reliable.
The men in the Russian army were so worn out by this continuous marching at twenty-seven miles a day that they simply could not go any faster.

To understand the degree of exhaustion of the Russian army, you only need to grasp the meaning of one fact: while losing no more than five thousand killed and wounded after Tarutino, and fewer than a hundred prisoners, the Russian army that had left Tarutino a hundred thousand strong reached Krasnoe with only fifty thousand.

The rapid Russian pursuit was just as destructive to our army as the French flight was to theirs. The only difference was that the Russian army moved voluntarily, without facing the total annihilation that threatened the French, and that sick Frenchmen were left behind in enemy hands while sick Russians were left among their own people. The main cause of Napoleon's army wasting away was the speed of its movement, and convincing proof of this is the corresponding decline of the Russian army.

Kutuzov, as far as it was in his power—instead of trying to check the French movement as was desired in Petersburg and by the Russian generals—directed all his efforts, as he had at Tarutino and Vyazma, toward speeding it along while easing the burden on his own troops.

But besides this, since the army's exhaustion and enormous reduction from the speed of the advance had become obvious, another reason presented itself for slowing down: the aim of the Russian army was to pursue the French. The French route was unknown, so the closer the Russians followed on their heels, the greater the distance they had to cover. Only by following at some distance could they cut across the French zigzag path. All the clever maneuvers suggested by the generals meant additional marches that would further lengthen the army's journey, whereas the only sensible objective was to shorten those marches. To this end, Kutuzov directed his efforts throughout the entire campaign from Moscow to Vilna—not casually or intermittently, but so consistently that he never once deviated from it.

Kutuzov felt and knew—not through reasoning or military science, but with every fiber of his Russian being—what every Russian soldier felt: that the French were beaten, that the enemy was fleeing and must be driven out; but at the same time he, like his soldiers, understood all the hardships of this unprecedented march.

But the generals—especially the foreign ones in the Russian army—who wanted to distinguish themselves and astonish someone, and for some reason capture a king or a duke, thought that now—when any battle would be horrible and senseless—was the perfect time to fight and conquer somebody. Kutuzov merely shrugged his shoulders when one after another they presented him with maneuver plans for soldiers who were ill-shod, barely clothed, and half-starved—soldiers who within a month, without fighting a single battle, had dwindled to half their original number and who, at best, still had farther to march than they already had before reaching the border.
This desire to distinguish themselves, to maneuver, to overthrow and cut off showed itself most clearly whenever the Russians stumbled on the French army.

So it was at Krasnoe, where they expected to find one of the three French columns but instead ran into Napoleon himself with sixteen thousand men. Despite all of Kutuzov's efforts to avoid this ruinous encounter and preserve his troops, the slaughter of the broken French mob by exhausted Russians continued at Krasnoe for three days.

Toll wrote out a battle plan: "The first column will march to such and such a place," and so on. And as usual, nothing happened according to plan. Prince Eugene of Wurttemberg fired from a hilltop at the French crowds running past and demanded reinforcements that never arrived. The French, avoiding the Russians, scattered and hid in the forest by night, making their way around as best they could, and continued their flight.

Miloradovich, who said he didn't want to know anything about commissary affairs and could never be found when needed—this self-styled knight without fear and without reproach who loved to parley with the French—sent envoys demanding their surrender, wasted time, and didn't do what he was ordered to do.
(Knight without fear and without reproach.)
"I give you that column, lads," he said, riding up to his troops and pointing out the French to the cavalry.

And the cavalry, with spurs and sabers urging on horses that could barely move, trotted with great effort to the column "presented" to them—that is, to a crowd of Frenchmen frozen stiff, frostbitten, and starving—and the column that had been "presented" threw down its arms and surrendered, as it had long been desperate to do.

At Krasnoe they took twenty-six thousand prisoners, several hundred cannon, and a stick called a "marshal's staff," and they argued about who had distinguished himself and congratulated themselves on their achievement—while deeply regretting that they hadn't captured Napoleon, or at least a marshal or some kind of hero, and blaming one another and especially Kutuzov for having failed to do so.

These men, carried away by their passions, were nothing more than blind tools of the most tragic law of necessity, yet they considered themselves heroes and imagined they were accomplishing a most noble and honorable deed. They blamed Kutuzov, saying that from the very start of the campaign he had prevented them from defeating Napoleon, that he only cared about his own comfort, that he had stopped the advance at Krasnoe because he lost his nerve on learning Napoleon was there, and that he probably had a secret agreement with Napoleon and had been bribed, and so on and so on.

Not only his contemporaries, carried away by their passions, but posterity and history itself have proclaimed Napoleon as "grand," while Kutuzov is described by foreigners as a crafty, dissolute, weak old courtier, and by Russians as something vague and indefinite—a sort of puppet useful only because he had a Russian name.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter V
paragraphs: In 1812 and 1813, Kutuzov was openly accused of blundering. The Emperor was dissatisfied with him. And in a history recently written by official command, it is stated that Kutuzov was a cunning court liar, terrified of Napoleon's name, and that by his blunders at Krasnoe and the Berezina he deprived the Russian army of the glory of a complete victory over the French.
(History of the Year 1812. The character of Kutuzov and reflections on the unsatisfactory results of the battles at Krasnoe, by Bogdanovich.)

Such is the fate—not of great men ("grands hommes") as the Russian mind does not acknowledge them—but of those rare and always solitary individuals who, perceiving the will of Providence, submit their personal will to it. The hatred and contempt of the crowd is the punishment for those who discern a higher law.

For Russian historians, strange and terrible to say, Napoleon—that most insignificant tool of history, who never anywhere, even in exile, showed human dignity—Napoleon is the object of admiration and enthusiasm; he is "grand." But Kutuzov—the man who from beginning to end of his activity in 1812 never once wavered by word or deed from Borodino to Vilna, who presented an example of self-sacrifice unmatched in history and a living awareness of the future significance of what was happening—Kutuzov seems to them something vague and pathetic, and when they speak of him and of the year 1812, they always seem a little embarrassed.

And yet it is hard to imagine a historical figure whose actions were so unwaveringly directed toward a single aim. And it would be hard to imagine any aim more worthy or more in harmony with the will of the entire people. Still harder would it be to find another instance in history where the aim of a historical figure was so completely accomplished as the aim to which all of Kutuzov's efforts were directed in 1812.

Kutuzov never spoke of "forty centuries looking down from the Pyramids," of the sacrifices he was making for the fatherland, or of what he intended or had accomplished. In general he said nothing about himself, struck no poses, always appeared to be the simplest and most ordinary of men, and said the simplest and most ordinary things. He wrote letters to his daughters and to Madame de Stael, read novels, enjoyed the company of pretty women, joked with generals, officers, and soldiers, and never contradicted anyone who tried to prove anything to him. When Count Rostopchin galloped up to Kutuzov at the Yauza bridge and personally accused him of causing Moscow's destruction, saying: "How could you promise not to abandon Moscow without a battle?" Kutuzov replied: "And I shall not abandon Moscow without a battle"—though Moscow was already abandoned. When Arakcheev, coming from the Emperor, told him that Ermolov ought to be appointed chief of artillery, Kutuzov replied: "Yes, I was just saying so myself"—though a moment before he had said the exact opposite. What did it matter to him—the only man amid a senseless crowd who understood the tremendous significance of what was happening—whether Rostopchin blamed him or himself for Moscow's destruction? Still less could it matter who was named chief of artillery.

Not only in these cases but constantly, that old man—who through long experience had reached the conviction that thoughts and the words expressing them are not what move people—used perfectly meaningless words that simply came into his head.

But that man, so careless with his words, never once during his entire period of activity uttered a single word inconsistent with the one aim toward which he worked throughout the whole war. Obviously, despite himself, in the most diverse circumstances, he repeatedly expressed his true convictions with the bitter certainty that he would not be understood. Beginning with the battle of Borodino, from which point his disagreement with those around him began, he alone said that Borodino was a victory, and he repeated this both verbally and in his dispatches and reports until his death. He alone said that the loss of Moscow did not mean the loss of Russia. In reply to Lauriston's proposal of peace, he said: There can be no peace, for such is the people's will. He alone, during the French retreat, said that all their maneuvers were useless, that everything was working out better than they could wish without them, that the enemy must be offered a "golden bridge," that the battles at Tarutino, Vyazma, and Krasnoe were unnecessary, that they needed to keep enough strength to reach the border, and that he would not sacrifice a single Russian for ten Frenchmen.

And this courtier, as he is portrayed—who lies to Arakcheev to please the Emperor—he alone, at the cost of the Emperor's displeasure, said in Vilna that to carry the war beyond the frontier was useless and harmful.

Nor do his words alone prove that he understood the meaning of events. His actions—without the slightest deviation—were all directed toward one and the same threefold end: (1) to concentrate all his strength for the conflict with the French, (2) to defeat them, and (3) to drive them out of Russia, while minimizing as far as possible the suffering of his people and his army.

This supposed procrastinator Kutuzov, whose motto was "Patience and Time," this supposed enemy of decisive action, gave battle at Borodino and invested the preparations for it with unparalleled solemnity. This Kutuzov, who before the battle of Austerlitz said it would be lost, he alone, contradicting everyone else, declared to his dying day that Borodino was a victory—despite the assurance of generals that the battle was lost and the unprecedented fact that an army had to retreat after winning. He alone, throughout the entire retreat, insisted that further battles were useless, that a new war should not be begun, and that the Russian frontier should not be crossed.

It is easy now to understand the significance of these events—if only we refrain from attributing to the actions of the masses aims that existed only in the heads of a dozen people—for the events and their results now lie before us.
But how did that old man, alone, in opposition to the general opinion, so accurately perceive the importance of the people's view of events that in all his actions he was never once untrue to it?
The source of that extraordinary power of insight lay in the national feeling that he possessed in full purity and strength.

Only the recognition that he possessed this feeling caused the people, in such a strange manner and contrary to the Tsar's wish, to choose him—an old man in disfavor—as their representative in the national war. And only that feeling placed him on the highest pedestal from which he, the commander in chief, devoted all his powers not to slaying and destroying men but to saving them and showing them pity.
That simple, modest, and therefore truly great figure could not be forced into the false mold of a European hero—the supposed ruler of men—that history has fabricated.
To a servant, no man can be great, because a servant has his own idea of what greatness means.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter VI
paragraphs: November fifth was the first day of what is called the battle of Krasnoe. Toward evening—after much arguing and many mistakes by generals who went to the wrong places, after adjutants had been sent racing about with counter-orders—when it became clear that the enemy was in full flight everywhere and that there could be no battle, Kutuzov left Krasnoe and went to Dobroe, where his headquarters had been transferred that day.

The day was clear and frosty. Kutuzov rode to Dobroe on his plump little white horse, followed by an enormous retinue of discontented generals who whispered among themselves behind his back. All along the road, groups of French prisoners captured that day—there were seven thousand of them—crowded around campfires to warm themselves. Near Dobroe, an immense crowd of tattered prisoners, buzzing with talk and wrapped and bandaged in whatever they could find, stood in the road beside a long row of unharnessed French guns. At the approach of the commander in chief, the buzz of talk ceased and all eyes turned to Kutuzov, who wore a white cap with a red band and a padded overcoat that bulged on his round shoulders as he moved slowly along the road on his white horse. One of the generals was reporting where the guns and prisoners had been captured.

Kutuzov seemed distracted and wasn't listening. He squinted with a dissatisfied expression as he studied the prisoners, who presented an especially wretched sight. Most of them were disfigured by frostbitten noses and cheeks, and nearly all had red, swollen, and festering eyes.

One group of Frenchmen stood close to the road, and two of them—one with his face covered in sores—were tearing at a piece of raw flesh with their hands. There was something horrible and animal-like in the fleeting glance they cast at the riders and in the hostile expression with which the soldier with the sores immediately turned away and went back to what he was doing.

Kutuzov looked long and hard at these two soldiers. He puckered his face, squinted, and pensively nodded his head. At another spot, he noticed a Russian soldier laughingly patting a Frenchman on the shoulder and saying something to him in a friendly way, and Kutuzov nodded his head again with the same expression.

"What were you saying?" he asked the general, who was continuing his report and directing the commander in chief's attention to some captured French standards standing before the Preobrazhensky regiment.
"Ah, the standards!" said Kutuzov, clearly pulling himself back with difficulty from the thoughts that preoccupied him.
He looked around absently. Thousands of eyes were watching him from all sides, waiting for a word from him.

He stopped in front of the Preobrazhensky regiment, sighed deeply, and closed his eyes. Someone on his staff beckoned to the soldiers carrying the standards to come forward and surround the commander in chief. Kutuzov was silent for several seconds, then, submitting with obvious reluctance to the duty imposed by his position, raised his head and began to speak. A crowd of officers gathered around him. He looked carefully at the circle of officers, recognizing several of them.

"I thank you all!" he said, addressing the soldiers and then the officers again. In the stillness around him, his slowly spoken words were clearly audible. "I thank you all for your hard and faithful service. The victory is complete, and Russia will not forget you! Honor to you forever."
He paused and looked around.

"Lower its head, lower it!" he said to a soldier who had accidentally lowered the French eagle he was holding in front of the Preobrazhensky standards. "Lower, lower, that's it. Hurrah, lads!" he added, with a quick motion of his chin.
"Hur-r-rah!" roared thousands of voices.
While the soldiers were shouting, Kutuzov leaned forward in his saddle and bowed his head, and his eye lit up with a mild and seemingly ironic gleam.

"You see, brothers..." he said when the shouts had died away... and all at once his voice and the expression on his face changed. It was no longer the commander in chief speaking but an ordinary old man who wanted to tell his comrades something very important.
A stir ran through the crowd of officers and the soldiers' ranks as they pressed forward to hear better what he was going to say.

"You see, brothers, I know it's hard for you, but it can't be helped! Bear up—it won't be long now! We'll see our visitors off and then we'll rest. The Tsar won't forget your service. It's hard for you, but still you're at home, while they—you see what they've come to," he said, pointing at the prisoners. "Worse off than our poorest beggars. While they were strong, we didn't spare ourselves, but now we can even pity them. They're human beings too. Isn't that right, lads?"

He looked around, and in the direct, respectful, wondering gazes fixed on him, he read agreement with what he had said. His face grew brighter and brighter with an old man's gentle smile, drawing the corners of his lips and eyes into a web of wrinkles. He stopped speaking and bowed his head as if in thought.
"But then again, who asked them to come here? Serves them right, the bloody bastards!" he suddenly cried, raising his head.
And flourishing his whip, he rode off at a gallop for the first time during the entire campaign, leaving behind the broken ranks of soldiers who were laughing joyfully and shouting "Hurrah!"

Kutuzov's actual words were barely understood by the troops. No one could have repeated the field marshal's speech, which began solemnly and ended as an old man's simple, heartfelt talk. But the genuine sincerity of that speech, the feeling of triumphant majesty combined with pity for the enemy and an awareness of the justice of their cause—expressed so perfectly by that old man's good-natured final outburst—was not merely understood but lived in the soul of every soldier and found expression in their joyous, prolonged cheering. Afterward, when one of the generals asked Kutuzov whether he wanted his carriage sent for, Kutuzov unexpectedly gave a sob in his reply, clearly deeply moved.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter VII
paragraphs: When the troops reached their night's stopping place on November eighth—the last day of the Krasnoe battles—it was already growing dark. All day it had been calm and frosty with occasional light snow, and toward evening the sky began to clear. Through the falling snow, a purple-black starry sky appeared and the frost grew sharper.

An infantry regiment that had left Tarutino three thousand strong but now numbered only nine hundred was one of the first to arrive at the halting place—a village on the highway. The quartermasters who met the regiment reported that all the huts were full of sick and dead Frenchmen, cavalrymen, and members of the staff. Only one hut was available for the regimental commander.
The commander rode up to his hut. The regiment passed through the village and stacked its arms in front of the last houses.

Like some huge, many-limbed animal, the regiment began to prepare its shelter and food. One part dispersed and waded knee-deep through snow into a birch forest to the right of the village, and immediately the sounds of axes, swords crashing through branches, and merry voices could be heard from there. Another group busied itself around the regimental wagons and horses, getting out kettles and hardtack and feeding the horses. A third section scattered through the village, arranging quarters for the staff officers, hauling out French corpses from the huts, and dragging away boards, dry wood, and thatch from the roofs for campfires, or fence panels for shelter.
About fifteen men with merry shouts were shaking down the tall wattle wall of a shed whose roof had already been removed.

"Now then, all together—push!" cried the voices, and the huge surface of the wall, sprinkled with snow and creaking with frost, swayed in the darkness of the night. The lower stakes cracked more and more, and finally the wall fell, along with the men who had been pushing it. Loud, rough laughter and joyous shouts followed.
"Now then, grab it in pairs! Hand up the lever! That's it... Where are you shoving?"
"Now, all together! But wait a moment, boys... With a song!"

Everyone fell silent, and a soft, pleasant, velvety voice began to sing. At the end of the third verse, as the last note died away, twenty voices roared out at once: "Oo-oo-oo-oo! That's it. All together! Heave away, boys!" But despite their combined efforts, the wattle hardly moved, and in the silence that followed, the heavy breathing of the men was the only sound.
"Hey, Sixth Company! You devils! Give us a hand... We might need you one of these days."

About twenty men from the Sixth Company, who were on their way into the village, joined the haulers, and the wattle wall—about thirty-five feet long and seven feet high—moved forward along the village street, swaying, pressing on and cutting into the shoulders of the gasping men.
"Get along... Falling? What are you stopping for? There now..."
Cheerful, meaningless abuse flowed freely.

"What do you think you're doing?" came the sharp, authoritative voice of a sergeant major who came upon the men hauling their load. "There are officers here! The general himself is in that hut, and you foul-mouthed brutes! I'll give it to you!" he shouted, hitting the first man he reached a swinging blow on the back. "Can't you keep it down?"
The men fell silent. The soldier who had been struck groaned and wiped his face, which had been scratched bloody when he fell against the wattle.
"There, see how that devil hits! He's made my face all bloody," he said in a frightened whisper when the sergeant major had passed.
"Don't you like it?" said a laughing voice, and lowering their tones, the men moved on.
Once they were out of the village, they began talking again just as loudly as before, larding their conversation with the same pointless profanity.

In the hut the men had passed, the senior officers had gathered and were in animated discussion over tea about the day's events and the maneuvers proposed for the next day. The plan was to make a flanking march to the left, cut off the Viceroy (Murat), and capture him.

By the time the soldiers had dragged the wattle fence into place, campfires were blazing on all sides. Wood crackled, snow melted, and black shadows of soldiers moved back and forth across the trampled area.

Axes and hatchets rang out everywhere. Everything was done without any orders being given. Firewood was gathered for the night, shelters were put up for the officers, kettles were boiling, and muskets and equipment were put in order.

The wattle wall the men had brought was set up in a semicircle by the Eighth Company as a windbreak against the north, propped up by musket rests, with a campfire built in front of it. They beat the evening drum, called the roll, had supper, and settled around the fires for the night—some mending their footwear, some smoking pipes, and some stripping naked to steam the lice out of their shirts.
